blurb: The showiest burnet, and the one that reads least like a burnet: long, slender, shaggy lilac-pink "squirrel tails" dangle from arching stems from midsummer into early autumn, each a mass of fine stamens, over a handsome mound of blue-green, deeply cut leaflets worth growing on its own. Longer, more slender and far more pendulous than the short, thick rose-pink brushes of Japanese burnet (S. obtusa) — but a cool mountain plant that wants steady moisture, not a Front Range xeric bed.
size: ~2–4 ft tall in flower × 2–3 ft wide
sun: Part shade here — morning sun with afternoon shade (full sun only where the soil stays reliably moist)
water: High — needs evenly moist soil that never dries out; NOT xeric, and not for a dry zone
spread: Slowly spreading from a rhizomatous, running rootstock; widens into a mat over years rather than running aggressively
seasons: Blue-green, deeply cut pinnate leaflets from spring; long, hanging lilac-pink "squirrel tails" on arching stems from midsummer into early autumn — longer, more slender and more pendulous than the shorter, thicker rose-pink brushes of Japanese burnet (S. obtusa), which also blooms earlier; dies to the ground in winter
wildlife: Late-season nectar and pollen for bees and butterflies; a wildlife-garden and prairie-planting perennial, and a good cut flower
deer: Burnets are generally rated deer-resistant, but no rating is published for this species — treat it as unproven here
toxic: No toxicity reported to people or pets — but no documented food use either
habitat: Alpine mountain ridges, sunny rock crevices and the grasslands beside them

care.hardiness: Cold is not this plant's problem here. It is a mountain perennial from the alpine ridges of Japan and Korea, and the Chicago Botanic Garden rates 'Lilac Squirrel' for USDA zones 4–10 — comfortably below Boulder's zone 5b–6a winter lows.[3][4] What limits it on the Front Range is the other end of the year: heat, dry air and soil that bakes dry. The RHS is explicit that it needs soil that does not dry out, so treat it as a cool-climate specialist that has to be sited and watered deliberately, not as a tough plant that will fend for itself.[1][2]
care.planting: Plant out in spring once the soil has warmed and the mid-May last frost has passed, so the roots have the whole season to establish before their first dry summer; early fall planting into cool, moist ground also works. Choose the coolest, moistest bed you have — an east- or north-facing border, a low spot that catches runoff, or the shaded side of taller plants — and work in generous organic matter before planting (see Soil).[1][2][7] In containers it is harder: pots in our sun and wind can dry out within a day, so use a large pot, a humus-rich mix and afternoon shade, and expect to water daily in July. Over winter, move the pot somewhere sheltered and keep it barely moist — a pot's rootball freezes far harder and dries out far faster than open ground.[1]
care.sun: The RHS rates it for full sun or partial shade, and in cool, cloudy maritime gardens full sun is genuinely fine.[1][2] That advice does not transfer to Boulder's thin, intense high-altitude sun. Give it morning sun with afternoon shade, or dappled light all day; the Chicago Botanic Garden's "full sun" listing assumes a Midwest summer with reliably moist soil.[3] In full afternoon sun here the leaf margins scorch and the flower stems wilt daily unless the soil is kept genuinely moist.[1][2]
care.soil: Moderately fertile, humus-rich, moist but well-drained soil that never dries out is the whole recipe.[1][2] The RHS rates it tolerant of clay, loam, sand and chalk and of acid, neutral or alkaline pH, so Boulder's alkaline reaction is not itself the obstacle — the obstacle is clay that bakes hard and dry through our summers.[1] Fix that with organic matter: CSU Extension recommends working 3–4 in of compost 8–12 in deep into a new bed (then about 0.25 in a year), aiming for 4–5% organic matter, which improves clay aggregation, porosity, drainage and rooting depth.[7] Then mulch, to hold onto the water you give it.
care.water: This is the make-or-break field. It is a moisture-loving mountain plant, not a xeric one, and the RHS requirement is soil that does not dry out.[1][2] Plan on a deep soak once or twice a week through a Boulder summer — more during a heat wave, and daily for anything in a pot — and put it on the wettest hydrozone of your irrigation, never in a dry or xeric bed. Mulch to slow evaporation. It also earns CSU's fall-and-winter watering routine: once or twice a month during long dry, snowless spells when the air is above 40°F, applied at midday so it soaks in before freezing, since herbaceous perennials in exposed, windy or southwest-facing spots are among the plants most hurt by our dry winters.[8]
care.spacing: Space plants roughly 2–2.5 ft apart. The RHS gives an ultimate height and spread of 1–1.5 m (3–5 ft) each way for 'Lilac Squirrel' under ideal conditions, though plants grown here usually stay nearer the low end.[1] Leave the flower stems room to arch, and give them something to lean on — the RHS notes the species may need support to keep from collapsing, so discreet ring stakes or close neighbours are worth planning for, especially on a plant grown lush and well watered.[2]
care.propagation: 'Lilac Squirrel' is a named cultivar and will not come true from seed — propagate it by division only, if you want the same plant.[1] The RHS advises dividing in spring or autumn: lift the clump, cut it into pieces each carrying several buds, and replant immediately into moist, amended soil, keeping the divisions well watered while they re-root.[1][2] Lifting and dividing every three or four years also keeps the clump vigorous. The straight species can be raised from seed if you simply want burnets rather than this selection,[2] and other burnets in the genus are also propagated by root and stem cuttings.[9]
care.bloom: Long, fluffy, pinkish-purple "squirrel tails" hang from arching stems from midsummer into early autumn — roughly July through September or October in a garden setting — which lands it squarely in the late-season gap after most perennials have finished.[1][3] The fuzz is stamens, not petals: burnet flowers have no true petals, and this species carries unusually long filaments, 6–10 mm against 1–3 mm in great burnet (S. officinalis), which is exactly why its tails read as shaggy rather than as tidy little bottlebrushes.[5] The stems also cut well for the vase.[1]
care.feeding: Keep fertility moderate — the RHS calls for a moderately fertile soil, not a rich one.[1] An annual spring mulch of compost, on top of the organic matter worked in at planting, is usually all it needs on Front Range clay; CSU notes that soils at 4–5% organic matter mineralize enough nitrogen that extra fertilizer is generally unnecessary.[7] Heavy feeding just pushes soft growth that flops.
care.maintenance: Most of the job is keeping the mulch topped up and the water steady. Cut the spent stems back in autumn, or leave the dark seedheads standing for a little structure and take them down in late winter — the RHS offers both.[2] Deadheading keeps the clump tidy through the bloom season, and dividing every three or four years keeps it flowering well.[1][2] Don't skip winter watering during dry, snowless stretches.[8]
care.troubles: The RHS reports it as generally pest-free and disease-free, and that matches its behaviour in gardens.[1] The troubles here are climatic rather than biological: scorched leaf margins and daily wilting when heat meets dry soil, and flower stems that flop when the plant is grown lush or in too much shade — support them if needed.[1][2] Sited in a dry, hot, unirrigated xeric bed it will simply fail. One label caveat: the RHS records this plant's name status as unresolved and lists Sanguisorba obtusa 'Lilac Squirrel' as a synonym, so you will also see it sold as Sanguisorba 'Lilac Squirrel' or under S. obtusa — the plant is the same, but check what you are actually buying against the long, pendulous flower tails, since true S. obtusa carries shorter, thicker pink bottlebrushes that open earlier, in June and July.[1][6]

edible.summary: Grown purely as an ornamental — no authority documents 'Lilac Squirrel' burnet as a food, so treat it as inedible.[1][2]
edible.caution: No horticultural or food-safety authority lists Sanguisorba hakusanensis as an edible plant. The RHS entries for the species and for 'Lilac Squirrel' cover it only as a garden perennial and record no edible use — and equally no toxicity warning.[1][2] A Korean national-biodiversity record, reported second-hand via Wikipedia, states that in South Korea the young leaves have been eaten and the roots used medicinally; the primary record could not be independently opened and verified from here, and a single ethnobotanical mention is not a food-safety source, so this guide does not treat the plant as edible.[4] Critically, do NOT reason across from salad burnet (Sanguisorba minor), the cucumber-scented culinary herb, or from great burnet (S. officinalis) — those are different species and edibility does not transfer between them. No significant toxicity is reported for this plant either, so a nibble is not an emergency, but the honest position is ornamental, not food. Nursery-grown plants may also carry pesticide residues.
